messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Frank is a 60-year-old man who has worked the same warehouse job for the last twenty years, a life of quiet routine that stands in stark contrast to the chaos that tore his youth apart. He has come to therapy at the urging of his partner, reporting decades of distress rooted in his service in Vietnam. The inciting event is a memory he has never been able to fully articulate. During a patrol in a dense jungle, his platoon was ambushed. The attack was sudden and overwhelming—a blur of noise, muzzle flashes in the green gloom, and the cries of his friends. He survived by diving into a ditch, where he lay motionless as the firefight raged and then fell silent. When he finally emerged, he was one of only three survivors in his platoon, surrounded by the bodies of men he considered brothers.

When the past intrudes on the present, it is not as a coherent story but as a sensory and emotional assault. Frank describes how the memory brings back the same raw terror he felt in that ditch, a physical certainty that his life is about to end. This terror is immediately followed by a wave of profound guilt, a feeling so potent it seems to curdle in his stomach. He has tried, on rare occasions, to explain it to his partner, but he finds he cannot find the words to describe what happened or the weight of having lived when so many others did not. The experience remains locked inside him, a silent horror film playing on a loop.

This visceral recall of the event consistently reinforces the dark conclusions he has drawn about himself and the world. Each time the terror and guilt resurface, it cements his belief that he is fundamentally damaged, a man who doesn't deserve the life he was given. He feels intense survival guilt, a conviction that it should have been him who died that day. In response to these terrifying memories, Frank has spent decades trying to outrun them. He assiduously avoids thinking about the event, changing the subject if anyone mentions the war and shutting down the television if a military documentary appears. This constant effort to suppress the past is his primary means of coping with the unbearable feelings the memories evoke.

Over time, these negative appraisals have become the lens through which he views his entire past, tainting even memories that should be neutral. The belief that he is a different, lesser person now makes him feel that the young man who went to war is a stranger he no longer recognizes. This sense of a fractured identity makes looking back at any part of his life feel painful and alien. Because he has come to believe the world is an irredeemably dangerous place and that he is permanently broken, he feels a desperate need to control his environment to prevent any reminders from breaking through. He refuses to go near the local VFW post, seeing it as a place saturated with the past he must avoid. Years ago, he threw out his old fatigues, and even now, the drab, olive-green of his work coveralls can feel uncomfortably heavy, a low-grade echo of the uniform he once wore.

This pattern of avoidance, meant to protect him, has only served to deepen his negative beliefs. By refusing to speak about his experiences, he has isolated himself, which strengthens his conviction that he is fundamentally alone and unknowable. The more he avoids places and thoughts connected to his past, the more powerful they seem, and the more fragile and incapable he feels in the present. At work, a loud bang from a dropped pallet can send a jolt of pure panic through him, and the subsequent shame he feels for this reaction in a mundane setting only confirms his belief that he is no longer the man he once was. The avoidance has become a cage, reinforcing the very appraisals that drive it.

It was after a car backfired on their street last month that his partner insisted he seek help. She found him frozen in the kitchen, pale and trembling, unable to speak. The fear in her eyes was more terrifying to him than his own. Frank has come to therapy not with any real hope of recovery, but with a deep weariness and the quiet fear that he has lost himself for good. He doesn't know who he would be without the guilt that has defined him for over forty years, and the thought of finding out is the most frightening prospect of all.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not describe how Frank's negative appraisals (e.g., 'I am damaged') influence or trigger his trauma memory.
